content: Basal body temperature (BBT) refers to the body temperature measured immediately upon waking, before engaging in any physical activity. In women, ovulation typically causes an increase in BBT by approximately 0.5 to 1 degree Fahrenheit (0.25 to 0.5 degrees Celsius). Tracking BBT is a method used to estimate the day of ovulation. Women generally exhibit a biphasic pattern in their BBT, characterized by lower temperatures before ovulation and higher temperatures afterward. Charting this biphasic pattern can be a useful tool in fertility awareness. The biphasic pattern is hormonally driven. During the pre-ovulatory (follicular) phase of the menstrual cycle, elevated estrogen levels suppress BBT. After ovulation, the corpus luteum releases progesterone, which raises BBT. The temperature rise is most commonly observed the day after ovulation, though this can vary. BBT tracking can only estimate ovulation within a three-day range. If pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum disintegrates, leading to a drop in BBT that coincides with the onset of menstruation. If pregnancy does occur, the corpus luteum remains functional and maintains elevated BBT levels throughout the first trimester. After the first trimester, the placenta assumes the functions of the corpus luteum, and the woman’s body temperature returns to pre-ovulatory levels. Rarely, the corpus luteum may form a cyst, which can cause prolonged elevation of BBT and delay menstruation until the cyst resolves, which may take weeks or months. For women trying to conceive, regular menstrual cycles are often interpreted as evidence of normal ovulation, while irregular cycles may suggest ovulatory dysfunction. However, many women with irregular cycles ovulate normally, and some with regular cycles may be anovulatory or have a luteal phase defect. BBT records can accurately determine whether a woman is ovulating and whether the luteal phase of her cycle is sufficiently long to support a pregnancy. Pregnancy tests are not reliable until 1–2 weeks after ovulation. Knowing the estimated date of ovulation can help prevent false-negative pregnancy test results caused by testing too early. Additionally, 18 consecutive days of elevated BBT strongly indicate pregnancy. Tracking BBT is a more accurate method of estimating gestational age than relying on menstrual period dates. For women avoiding pregnancy, charting BBT is used in some fertility awareness methods to identify the onset of post-ovulatory infertility. However, BBT only indicates when ovulation has already occurred; it does not predict ovulation. Since sperm can survive for up to five days, predicting ovulation several days in advance is necessary for effective pregnancy avoidance. BBT methods often incorporate rules similar to those of the Calendar Method to estimate the beginning of the pre-ovulatory fertile phase.
